simpleDefinition: A rule that says your fund manager can only charge a performance fee when your portfolio hits a new all-time high. If the fund drops 10% and recovers 8%, no performance fee — you're still under water.
proDefinition: Cumulative high-water mark provision. Performance fees only accrue on excess returns above the prior peak NAV / portfolio value. Prevents managers from re-earning fees on recovery from drawdowns.
whyItMatters: Without a high-water mark, you pay performance fees twice on the same gain after a drawdown.

simpleDefinition: When a fund stops accepting new investors (or new money) because it's reached a size where adding more would hurt returns. A sign of capacity discipline.
proDefinition: Voluntary halt of new subscriptions, typically at a strategy-specific AUM threshold beyond which alpha generation degrades. Common in concentrated small/mid-cap PMS and Cat III alpha-seeking AIFs.
whyItMatters: Funds that soft-close often outperform funds that scale endlessly — capacity discipline is a quality signal.

simpleDefinition: A clause that lets the fund manager 'catch up' to a higher fee share once they cross the hurdle rate. Aggressive — they end up earning fees on the entire return, not just the part above the hurdle.
proDefinition: Fee provision (typically 50-100% catch-up) where, after returns clear the hurdle, the manager retains all or most subsequent returns until they reach their full fee share on the entire return. Subtle but materially fee-additive.
whyItMatters: A 100% catch-up clause turns a 'fair' 15% performance fee above 10% hurdle into something much closer to 15% on everything.

simpleDefinition: A Private Placement Memorandum is the legal document an AIF gives you before you invest. It spells out strategy, fees, risks, and the exit terms. Read it cover-to-cover before signing anything.
proDefinition: Private Placement Memorandum. SEBI-mandated disclosure document for AIFs. Covers investment strategy, target returns, fee schedule, redemption terms, side-letter policies, conflicts of interest, and risk factors.
whyItMatters: If you haven't read the PPM, you don't know what you've actually committed to.

simpleDefinition: The year a closed-ended fund (typically AIF) starts deploying capital. Different vintages perform very differently — investing across multiple years smooths the ride.
proDefinition: The cohort year when a closed-ended fund begins capital deployment. Vintage-year diversification mitigates dispersion risk in PE / VC / RE strategies where outcomes are heavily entry-period dependent.
whyItMatters: Two AIFs with the same strategy and manager can return wildly different numbers based purely on what year they deployed.

simpleDefinition: A PMS where the manager can buy and sell on your behalf without asking you each time. Most PMS in India is discretionary.
proDefinition: PMS structure where the portfolio manager has full investment authority within the agreed mandate. Contrasts with non-discretionary PMS (advisory) where each transaction requires client consent.
whyItMatters: Discretionary speeds execution but demands you trust the manager — you'll see trades only after they happen.

simpleDefinition: A PMS where the manager only suggests trades — you have to approve each one. Slower, but you stay in the driver's seat.
proDefinition: Advisory PMS structure requiring client consent for each transaction. Less common today than discretionary; preferred by sophisticated investors who want execution support without surrendering decision authority.
whyItMatters: You retain control, but you're also the bottleneck — execution lag matters in volatile markets.

simpleDefinition: A way to ring-fence illiquid or troubled holdings inside a fund so they don't drag down NAV calculations or new investors' pricing.
proDefinition: Segregated portfolio sub-vehicle for illiquid, defaulted, or distressed assets. Removes valuation uncertainty from the main fund while preserving recovery upside for original holders.
whyItMatters: Side pockets protect existing investors but signal stress — ask why they were created.

simpleDefinition: Internal Rate of Return is the annualised return for a fund where money goes in and comes out at different times. Standard for closed-ended AIFs and PE funds.
proDefinition: Internal Rate of Return. The discount rate that makes the NPV of all cash flows zero. Time-weighted differently from CAGR — handles staged drawdowns and irregular distributions, making it the dominant metric for closed-ended PE / VC / Cat II AIFs.
whyItMatters: CAGR works for open-ended funds; IRR is mandatory for closed-ended ones with capital calls.

simpleDefinition: Total Value to Paid-In is a closed-ended fund metric that says, 'For every ₹1 you invested, the fund's current value plus distributions is ₹X.' A TVPI of 2.5x means you've made 1.5x your money so far.
proDefinition: Total Value to Paid-In Capital. (Distributed value + remaining NAV) / total capital called. Standard PE / VC reporting metric alongside DPI (Distributed to Paid-In) and IRR.
whyItMatters: TVPI captures unrealised plus realised — useful for partway-through closed-ended funds.

simpleDefinition: Distributions to Paid-In is what you've actually received in cash, divided by what you put in. A DPI of 1.0x means you've gotten your money back; >1.0x means you're in profit.
proDefinition: Distributed value to Paid-In capital. Cash returns realised, divided by capital called. The 'cash on cash' metric for closed-ended funds — distinct from TVPI which includes unrealised NAV.
whyItMatters: DPI is the only PE metric you can spend — TVPI on paper is not money in your account.

simpleDefinition: When the fund manager invests their own personal money alongside yours in the same fund. A strong sign of skin in the game.
proDefinition: Personal capital commitment by the GP / portfolio manager into the same vehicle, usually 1-5% of fund size. Critical alignment signal especially for Cat I/II AIFs and concentrated PMS.
whyItMatters: A manager who won't co-invest in their own strategy is asking you to take a risk they won't.

simpleDefinition: Know Your Customer is the SEBI-mandated identity verification you complete before investing in any market product. PAN, address proof, photo — once done, valid across all SEBI-registered intermediaries.
proDefinition: Centralised KYC under the SEBI / KRA framework. One-time verification using PAN, address, and bank documentation, valid across all SEBI intermediaries. Periodic re-verification required for material change events.
whyItMatters: KYC is the on-ramp — without it you can't invest in PMS, AIF, MF, or even open a demat.

simpleDefinition: An electronic account where your shares, bonds, and PMS holdings are stored. PMS portfolios sit in your own demat — you can see every trade as it happens.
proDefinition: Dematerialised securities account held with NSDL or CDSL via a Depository Participant. PMS uses individual demats (not pooled) — providing transparency and tax-clarity that AIFs cannot match.
whyItMatters: Your PMS holdings are visible in your demat — that's the fundamental difference from a mutual fund or AIF.

simpleDefinition: An independent entity (often a bank) that holds your AIF assets in trust on behalf of investors. They verify the fund manager isn't doing anything outside the agreed strategy.
proDefinition: Independent trustee bank under the AIF trust structure. Holds title to fund assets, validates compliance with PPM-stated strategy, and ratifies certain manager actions. Key operational-risk safeguard.
whyItMatters: A weak trustee weakens the whole AIF — check who it is before committing.

simpleDefinition: The bank or institution that physically holds your fund's assets — separate from the fund manager. Independent custody means even if the manager fails, your assets are still there.
proDefinition: Independent custodian holding fund securities and managing settlement. Mandatory for AIFs and most PMS. Top-tier custodians (HDFC, Citi, Deutsche Bank) carry stronger track records than smaller domestic players.
whyItMatters: A weak custodian is the operational risk most investors don't think about until something goes wrong.

simpleDefinition: An Asset Management Company is the entity that runs mutual funds, PMS, and SIFs. SEBI-licensed, with strict capital and governance requirements.
proDefinition: Asset Management Company. SEBI-registered entity authorised to run mutual fund schemes, PMS strategies, and (post-2024) SIF products. Subject to capital adequacy, fit-and-proper, and key-person rules.
whyItMatters: The AMC name on the door tells you about governance and operational depth — small AMCs aren't bad, but they require more diligence.

simpleDefinition: A Registered Investment Adviser is a SEBI-licensed advisor who can charge you fees for advice but cannot earn commissions from products. The opposite of a distributor.
proDefinition: Registered Investment Adviser under SEBI's 2013 RIA regulations. Fee-only or fee-and-commission RIAs differ; pure fee-only RIAs cannot accept any product-side incentive. Stricter conflict-of-interest rules than distributors.
whyItMatters: Fee-only RIAs are conflict-free — distributor advice is shaped by what they earn from each product.

simpleDefinition: An intermediary who places mutual fund or PMS products with you and earns a commission from the AMC. Their advice is shaped by who pays them — not necessarily by what's best for you.
proDefinition: AMFI-registered or SEBI-recognised distributor. Earns trail and one-time commissions from the product manufacturer. Subject to disclosure rules but not the strict conflict-of-interest standards that apply to RIAs.
whyItMatters: Free advice is rarely free — it's paid for by the product, which means it cannot be unbiased.

simpleDefinition: How much a fund's returns deviate from its benchmark, measured as a percentage. Lower = closer to the index. PMS and active funds intentionally have higher tracking error.
proDefinition: Standard deviation of the difference between fund returns and benchmark returns over time. Measures the consistency of active deviation. Active strategies need higher tracking error to generate alpha; passive strategies aim for near-zero.
whyItMatters: Tracking error tells you whether the manager is actually doing something different — or just paying you to closet-track the index.

simpleDefinition: The excess return your manager generates above the benchmark, after accounting for risk. If the Nifty did 12% and your PMS did 16% with similar risk, that's 4% alpha.
proDefinition: Risk-adjusted excess return over benchmark. Often computed via Jensen's alpha or as residual after factor-model adjustment. Genuine alpha is rare and persists less than most marketing decks suggest.
whyItMatters: Past alpha rarely repeats. Demand evidence of process, not just historical numbers.

simpleDefinition: How much a fund moves with the market. A beta of 1.0 means it tracks the market 1:1; below 1.0 is less volatile, above is more.
proDefinition: Sensitivity coefficient relating asset returns to market returns. β = Cov(Ri,Rm) / Var(Rm). Used in CAPM to decompose returns into market exposure plus alpha.
whyItMatters: High-beta funds amplify both gains and losses — match beta to your stomach, not just the headline return.

simpleDefinition: A measure of return per unit of risk. Higher is better. A Sharpe of 1.0 is decent, 2.0 is excellent, below 0.5 means you're not being paid enough for the risk.
proDefinition: (Return − Risk-Free Rate) / Volatility. Ratio of excess return per unit of total risk (standard deviation). Standard risk-adjusted measure but penalises upside volatility equally with downside.
whyItMatters: Funds with similar returns but very different Sharpe ratios behave very differently when markets fall.

simpleDefinition: Like Sharpe ratio, but only penalises downside volatility (not all wobbles). A better measure for asymmetric strategies.
proDefinition: (Return − Risk-Free Rate) / Downside Deviation. Refinement of Sharpe that penalises only below-target returns. Preferred for skewed strategies — long-short, options-heavy, distressed credit.
whyItMatters: For strategies that aim for asymmetric upside, Sortino is more informative than Sharpe.

simpleDefinition: The biggest peak-to-trough fall the fund has ever experienced. The single most predictive number for whether you'll panic-sell.
proDefinition: Largest cumulative percentage decline from peak NAV / portfolio value over a measurement window. More behaviorally predictive than volatility — investors panic at drawdowns, not at standard deviation.
whyItMatters: You won't quit at high standard deviation. You'll quit at drawdown — know yours in advance.

simpleDefinition: Returns calculated for every possible 3-year (or 5-year) period, not just the last one. Hides the lottery effect of one good year and shows what you'd typically have earned.
proDefinition: Time-series of period-shifted returns over fixed horizons (e.g., 3-year rolling). Eliminates point-in-time bias inherent in trailing-period reporting and surfaces the dispersion an investor would actually have experienced.
whyItMatters: Trailing 5-year returns are one number; rolling 5-year returns are dozens — and the dispersion is the real story.

simpleDefinition: A Non-Resident Ordinary account is the rupee account NRIs use to manage Indian-source income (rent, dividends, etc.). Repatriation is capped at $1M per financial year.
proDefinition: Non-Resident Ordinary rupee account. Used by NRIs / OCIs for Indian-source income. Repatriation subject to RBI's $1M / FY limit and post-tax requirement; balances are non-interest-repatriable beyond cap.
whyItMatters: For NRIs, the NRO is the limiting factor — most onshore PMS / MF flows route through it.

simpleDefinition: A Non-Resident External account is the freely repatriable rupee account NRIs use for foreign-source income brought to India. Whatever you put in, you can take out, no $1M cap.
proDefinition: Non-Resident External rupee account. Holds rupee balance funded only from foreign currency. Both principal and interest are freely repatriable, with no FY cap.
whyItMatters: For NRIs who want flexibility, NRE is the cleaner route — but you can only fund it with foreign-earned money.

simpleDefinition: A Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) deposit lets NRIs hold deposits in USD, GBP, EUR, etc. — no INR currency risk. Repatriable, but rates are usually lower than rupee deposits.
proDefinition: FCNR(B) deposit. Term deposit denominated in permitted foreign currencies (USD, GBP, EUR, JPY, AUD, CAD). Tenure 1-5 years, fully repatriable, exempt from currency conversion risk for the depositor.
whyItMatters: FCNR is the cleanest way for NRIs to lock in INR-free returns onshore — rates are softer but currency risk is zero.

simpleDefinition: Passive Foreign Investment Company is a US tax classification that hits Indian mutual funds and most AIFs hard for US taxpayers. Annual reporting + punitive tax — usually a deal-breaker for US-resident NRIs.
proDefinition: US Internal Revenue Code sections 1291-1298. Most non-US mutual funds and pooled vehicles trigger PFIC status for US taxpayers, requiring annual Form 8621, mark-to-market or QEF elections, and punitive default taxation otherwise.
whyItMatters: For US-tax-resident NRIs, PFIC rules eliminate most onshore Indian mutual fund / AIF strategies — GIFT City structures sidestep this.

simpleDefinition: Securities Transaction Tax is a small tax (0.001-0.1%) on every equity trade in India. Hidden cost, but high-turnover PMS strategies feel it more than buy-and-hold ones.
proDefinition: Securities Transaction Tax. 0.001% to 0.1% (varying by instrument and side) charged on listed equity, derivatives, and ETF transactions. Not deductible for income tax but counted in the long-term capital gains computation eligibility.
whyItMatters: STT is small, but multiplied by turnover, it's a real fee for high-churn PMS strategies.

simpleDefinition: Goods and Services Tax adds 18% on top of management and performance fees you pay to your PMS or AIF. Always confirm whether quoted fees are inclusive or exclusive of GST.
proDefinition: Indirect tax of 18% applied to financial advisory and asset management services in India. Levied on the AMC's invoice to the client. Not creditable / refundable for retail investors.
whyItMatters: A '2% management fee' is really 2.36% with GST — quoted fees almost always exclude it.

simpleDefinition: A fund that doesn't pick stocks itself — it picks other funds. Adds diversification but also a second layer of fees.
proDefinition: FoF structure. Single vehicle holding stakes across multiple underlying funds. Useful for smaller allocators wanting diversified PE / VC / credit exposure but stacks fees (management at FoF + management at underlying).
whyItMatters: Fund of funds means double fees — make sure the diversification is worth the cost layer.

simpleDefinition: Investing in closed-ended funds across multiple deployment years instead of all in one year. Reduces the risk that a single year's market mood determines your outcomes.
proDefinition: Allocation strategy of staggering commitments across 3-5 successive vintage years to mitigate dispersion. Standard practice for institutional PE / VC programmes; less common but increasingly relevant for HNI AIF investors.
whyItMatters: Vintage diversification is to AIFs what SIPs are to mutual funds — it removes a timing risk you can't predict.

simpleDefinition: The set of numbers — drawdown, volatility, Sharpe, beta — that describe how risky a fund actually is. A fund that won't disclose these is hiding something.
proDefinition: Standard fund-disclosure pack: trailing returns, max drawdown, volatility, Sharpe / Sortino, alpha / beta vs benchmark, downside capture. SEBI does not mandate uniform disclosure outside MFs, so PMS / AIF rigour varies.
whyItMatters: Returns alone don't tell you anything. Risk metrics turn 'great track record' into 'great risk-adjusted track record'.
